"The Constitution does not create an obligation that the political party 
forming the ministry should necessarily have a majority in the 
Legislature. 
Minority governments are not unknown. What is necessary is that 
government should enjoy the confidence of the House. Secondly and 
more importantly whether the council of ministers has lost the

action. It is not for the Governor to determine the said question on his 
own or on his own verfication. This is not a matter within his 
subjective satisfaction. It is an objective fact capable of being 
established on the floor of the House.

pervasive violence, the Governor comes to the conclusion and 
records the same in his report-that for the reasons mentioned by him, 
a free vote is not possible in the House."

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
the imposition of President's Rule in Uttar Pradesh has once again raised the 
issue of the role of the Governors in discharging their Constitutional 
responsibilities. Two arguments have been raised. One is that there is no 
option for the Governor. I disagree with  that. There was a democratic option to 
call the single largest party to form a popular Government. The Governor has 
not done that. The second was that if  the President's Rule had not been 
imposed, there would have been possibilit ies of horse -trading. What is the 
present situation? Now already the President's Rule is there. The Assembly is 
kept in suspended animation. What is the aim of this? Already one of the MLAs 
of the Smajwadi Party was shot dead in the precincts of the Governor's 
residence. So, if that is the argument, then what is the purpose of this keeping 
the Assembly in suspended animation? Sir, the incidents in Uttar Pradesh 
raise three important issues. One is, w hat is the option before the Governor 
when only one political party alone stakes its claim to form a Government. No 
Other political party except the Smaj wadi Party made its claim before the 
Governor to form a Govern ment. In the Uttar Prades h elections, no political 
party got an absolute majority. But the Smajwadi Party emerged as the single 
largest party. It staked its claim before the Governor and asked for time to 
prove its majority. The other two larger parties next to Smajwadi Party, the 
BSP and the BJP did not stake their claim.  In such a situation, what is the 
option before the Governor? He should allow the Smajwadi Party to form the 
Government and ask it to prove its majority in the Assembly. The Governor did 
not do that. In democratic polity, the attempt should always be made to form a 
popular Government. But this possibility was not explored by Governor in Uttar 
Pradesh. The second important issue is, the democratic convention. I do agree 
that there were violations. But the over all conventions insist that the single 
largest party should be called to form the Government.   Actually,

SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (P ondicherry): I thank you, Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. 
The Short Duration Discussion is on the role of Governors in 
discharging their constitutional responsibilities in the formation of 
Governments in States, in the light of  the recent events in Uttar Pradesh. 
Almost everybody who spoke before me made quotations from the Report 
102 

[11 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
of the Sarkaria Commission. I am also bound to quote a few observations of 
the Commission.  At page 135 of the Report, it is said: 
"(b) If there is a single party having an absolute majority in the Assembly, the 
leader of the party should automatically be asked to become the Chief 
Minister. 
If there is no such party, the Governor should select a Chief Minister from 
among the following parties or groups of parties by sounding them, in turn, in 
the order of preference indicated below: 
(ii) The largest single party staking a claim to form the government with the 
support of others, including  independents." 
If one of the largest parties, in the case of U.P., is staking a claim 
that it can form the government, it has to be called, going by the observations 
of the Sarkaria Commission. 
The Report further says that the Governor is not entitled to ascertain 
whether there is a majority or not on his own. It can be ascertained only on the 
floor of the Assembly.  The Report, at page 136, states: 
"The Governor should not risk determining the issue of majority 
support, on his own, outside the Assembly. The prudent course for him would 
be to cause the rival claims to be tested on the floor of the House." 
In the present case, it has not been so determined by the Governor. 
In reality, not calling the single largest party to form the government is a 
mistake committed by the Governor. The Governor ought to have called the 
single largest party in U.P. to form the government. 
As my learned friend, Mr. Ramachandran Pillai, has pointed out, it is 
not a novel thing that has happened in  the present case alone. It happened in 
Tamil Nadu, in West Bengal and even here in 1996, when a minority 
Government was formed--what happened subsequently, of course, is a 
different matter. There are a lot of precedents as to the largest party being 
called to form the government. The largest single party ought to have been 
called by the Governor in the present case also. In such cases, traditions   and   
conventions   have   a   major   role  to  play.      Neither  the 
103 

RAJYA SABHA        [11 MARCH, 2002] 
Constitution, nor any report of any Commi ttee, insists that only the party or 
group enjoying a majority should be called to form the government. Nowhere is 
it said in the Constitution that the party which is having a majority alone should 
be called to form the government. On the other hand, we are having some sort 
of guidelines given by the Sarkaria Commission. 
It was argued here that there might be some horse-trading before the 
government is formed. As long as ther e are horses, there will be trading. We 
cannot prevent it. Once you have a gap of six months to form a government by 
either of the parties, there will be some sort of trading. As is well known, even 
in Rajya Sabha elections, there is a lot of horse-trading. That is why they are 
asking for open election of Rajya Sabha Members. My submission is, since we 
are not having any specific guidelines in these cases, except the Report of the 
Sarkaria Commission, we have to go to the Supreme Court. As happened in 
the S.R. Bommai case, somebody shou ld go to the Supreme Court, seeking 
directions as to what we have to do when there is no majority at all. 
In this respect, necessary guidelines should be obtained from the 
Supreme Court itself as to how the Government can be formed when there is 
only a single largest party. Thank you. 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu):  Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. at 
the outset, I would like to say that the decision on imposition of the President's 
rule in U.P. is wrong. It will create a wrong precedent for future. The single 
largest party should be given the first chance to form the Government. This is 
the established norm and healthy practice. But, on the face of it, the 
Governor's decision to recommend the Pres ident's rule in t he State, without 
giving any opportunity to any party to prove its majority on the floor of the 
House, seems to be a hurried one. I feel  that the Governor had taken this 
decision without giving proper thought to  the point at issue. In the famous 
Bommai case, the Supreme Court had laid down that the Assembly is the 
proper place to test and prove the majority. In this case, the Governor failed to 
follow this principle which had been taid down by the Supreme Court in 
Bommai's case. Sir, fractured verdicts and coalition Governments are now the 
order of the day, not only in India, but also in other countries. The State of 
Manipur which had gone to the polls alon g with U.P. was the latest example 
where a coalition Government has come 
to power.  Sir,  the leader of the Samajwadi Party, Shri Mulayam Singh 
 
104 

[11 MARCH. 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Yadav, had staked his claim to form the Government, and he was ready to 
prove his majority on the floor of the House. The Governor should have given 
the first chance to a leader of the single largest party to form the Government 
in UP. We do not know why he has not given this opportunity to Shri Mulayam 
Singh Yadav to form the Government. In this case, the Governor himself came 
to the wrong conclusion that no party  in U.P. was able to form a stable 
Government. Without following the established norms and procedure, the 
Governor has recommended the Central ru le in U.P. Moreover, in U.P. the 
Assembly has been placed under suspended animation. This will give room 
for horse-trading and unwanted practice. This decision will further complicate 
the situation. So, the Governor and th e Government of India should have 
handled this situation properly, so as to  ensure the dignity of the system of 
parliamentary democracy as well as th e rule of law. Hence, I oppose the 
imposition of President's rule in U.P. Thank you.

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI

Assembly. Even out of a hung Assembly , as the hon. Member from the DMK,

hung Assemblies, a combination enjoying a majority support can, actually, 
emerge. But if such a situation does not happen and this hung Assembly does 
not produce a majority Government, on the contrary, it produces something 
which is detrimental to democracy, th en there is a deadlock. And, in a 
deadlock situation, as some Members hav e very honestly confessed, different 
combinations may not be prepared to have alliances or post-poll alliances, 
may stand on their original, rigid, posi tions and the arithmetic may be such 
that no one group can, actually, touch t he 50 per cent mark or even cross it. 
Commenting, in abstract, on the Repor t of the Governor may be one aspect. 
But let me just place three or four  facts before I comment on what the 
Constitutional and legal precedents in this area have been and should be. The 
National Democratic Alliance in Uttar Pradesh, led by Shri Raj Nath Singh, 
has 108 seats; the Bahujan Samaj Party, led by Ms. Mayawati, has won 98 
seats. The total strength of the Assembly is 403. Subsequently, one Member

still withheld. 
The functional strength of the Assembly is 399. The Governor invited 
the National Democratic Alliance partners for consultations; he invited Miss 
Mayawati; both were very categorical, oral ly and in writing, that they were not 
in any way going to support a Government led by Shri Mulayam Singh Yadav 
or the Samajwadi Party; they were opposed to any such combination. 
Therefore, two political groups, whic h comprised 206 out of 399, that is, a 
clear majority, gave in writing to the Governor that they were

not going to support a Government led by the Samajwadi Party. Mr. Mulayam 
Singh Yadav called on the Governor. He presented a list of his party's 143 
MLAs. which has now, unfortunately, be en reduced to 142, plus two of the 
CPI(M) -- at that time, 145; now 144. Now, how do you intend to cover this gap 
between 200 and 145; please give a list. Despite the Governor asking for a

letter of support to anobody has been given; no stand has been clarified. So, 
after exploring all opportunities and trying all options, the Governor is faced 
with a situation where the largest single  party is not short, but way, way short 
of the majority figure. As against 200 required, he cannot cross beyond 145. 
Those with an absolute majority in the Assembly, those separate groups -- 
groups disagreeing with each other -- give  in writing that "we are not going to 
support this Government", and, therefor e, it was not merely a situation of a 
hung Assembly, of which some magical solution could come out and suddenly 
this 145 could become 200; it was a si tuation where the majority mandates a 
clear 'no' against the Samajwadi Party in writing and orally -- public stand; 
written stand before the Governor. The overwhelming majority in the Assembly 
says 'not this Government' in writing and the man who claims majority is 
unable to show a list; even with the 25 of the Congress Party, it could have 
touched closer to some 170, but it would have been still short of the halfway

political formulations come up in future; maybe, they do not; but since we are 
living in a democracy where we are ruled by majority rule, the mandate must

step which the Governor has taken.   And it is not the first time.    Examples 
are given of

1996, in Uttar Pradesh; before that, in Kerala. Mr. Pillai gave that example. 
The 1965 elections in Kerala did not throw a clear mandate and, therefore, 
immediately after the election, when no body had a majority, there was a clear 
deadlock; a combination having a majority was also not possible. After the 
elections, no popular Government could be formed and, therefore, recourse 
was taken immediately after that, to article 356. In 1971, in Orissa, again, a 
deadlocked Assembly was thrown up by the electorate. 
No one group or a combination of groups of any formulation could 
have a majority. Attempts were made; but those attempts failed, and even

Governor, again recommended, suspended animation of the Assembly. So, 
you had three clear precedents. You had it  in Kerala; you had it in Orissa; you

we grapple with them? My friend, Mr.  Rajiv Shukla, suggested one solution

it." But, that was on a different issue. The judges then suggested a new 
solution altogether, and they said, "Call a session of the Assembly and let the 
Assembly directly elect a leader or a Government." Now, whether in a 
parliamentary democracy, where you have a ruling party which has to form a 
Government and an Opposition, such a formulation under our system is

like to examine it." It stayed the operatio n of the judgment. Therefore, in U.P. 
we are faced with a situation where the arithmetic figure is such that a 
deadlock has been created.   In  this  deadl ock,   the  Governor  really  had   
no  option   but  to

recommend that the Assembly be put  under suspended animation, and, 
therefore, it has been put under suspe nded animation. If a political formulation

Sir, when we are faced with or stared at by these facts, what does the 
Governor do? What is the legal position? One statement which was made was, 
there was no concept of majority rule mentioned in the Constitution. But, in a 
parliamentary democracy, where a Govern ment or a Council of Ministers is 
responsible to the House of People at the Centre and the Assembly in the 
State, article 164(2) has been very clearly interpreted what this responsibility to 
the Assembly means, or, what this res ponsibility to the House of the People 
means, that you must command the majority confidence. A Government per se 
must ordinarily have a majority. There is only one exception to this, and that 
one exception to the rule of majority in  a Government being, even if you don't 
have a majority, a minority Government ma y continue, if the majority in the 
House gives it a mandate to continue.' That is to say, "We know you don't 
have a majority, but we feel that imme diately there should be no elections. So, 
for one year, we are even going to allow a minority Government to continue." 
The illustration was given from 1969 to 1971. In British democracy, there are 
precedents where minority Governments have continued not on the principle 
that a minority can rule, but on the prin ciple that the majority has permitted the 
minority to rule. That also has a majority  mandate. That is the only principle in 
parliamentary democracy where you can have a minority Government which 
can actually function. 
So, how do we test the action of the Governor? Has this action been 
particularly fair? Or, is it partisan? The view which he has taken; is it a 
plausible view? Has he explored all the options? Did he have extensive 
consultation with the political parties? Ev en after doing this, if the Governor is

no option but to make the kind of recommendation which he has made.

[11 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Sir, comparisons have been made with the situation in 1996 at the 
Centre. My friend, Rajiv Shukla, has said that he considered the 1996 
precedent wrong and the 1998 precedent, where the President take letters of 
support, to be more correct. That may be his view. But let us bear in mind two 
factors. Even when we cite the 1996 precedent, the first is that, 
Constitutionally, there is a distincti on between a Government at the Centre 
and a Government in the State. If there is  no popular, elected, Government in 
the State, the Constitution envisages President's rule in that situation, and the 
administration can be carried on, under the President's rule. So, there can be 
a State, envisaged under our Constituti onal scheme, where there may be no 
elected Government, for some reason, there is a breakdown of Constitutional 
machinery or the governance can't be carried out in accordance with the 
Constitution. 
At the Centre, there is no such pr ovision. The Centre must always 
have a Government; there is no President's rule. This is one basic distinction. 
At the Centre, there can also be, conceivably, a minority Government, apart 
from ruling with the majority sanction. The moment the Government at the 
Centre loses its vote of confidence, t he Government goes; but it continues as 
a caretaker, as it happened in 1998, when the minority Government, led by 
Shri Vajpayee, continued, because the Centre has to have a Government, 
pending the holding of elections. So, you can always have a minority 
Government, if there is no popular Government possible. You can have a 
minority Government, pending the holding of  elections, as far as the Centre is 
concerned; because the centre must necessarily have a Government, but the 
position is different, as far as the State is concerned. 
Secondly, even in 1996, if we recolle ct-l think, I am not inaccurate; I 
can say from my memory--a combination, commanding a majority, saying that 
we don't want so and so and we are prepared to express our vote of 
confidence in so and so, didn't reac h the President. The President had only 
the claims and the figures. The President didn't have an alternative option 
before him. Here, the alternative combin ation, which was 206 out of 399, had

Government can never have a majority in the Assembly. These are all 
academic, abstract, discussions. 
Even under this situation, what does the Governor do? This leaves

the floor test, there is a distinction th ere between the article 356 situation, 
where you use it against the Government which has lost the majority, as 
against the Government whom you are inviting to prove its majority, except in 
exceptional situation, which is also mentioned, the ordinary rule is, the 
Governor must direct the Chief Minister and advise him to call the Assembly

the support of only 35% of the MLAs, and he can't reach even 36%, should he

when Justice Sarkaria in those instruct ions and guidelines when he mentions, 
it is very clear whether you call a single party or the emphasis is on or you call 
a single party with support of other part ies or independents, that can never be 
interpreted that Sarkaria Commission's mandate is that install a minority 
Government even when majority gives in writing that we are against it. We 
have been mentioning it. So, I will just like to read out one or two paragraphs 
from the Bommai Judgement case. Not one but various judges had the 
opportunity to deal with this issue. Bommai case was also not about inviting 
somebody to form a Gove rnment. It was a case where an existing Chief 
Minister lost the majority. I will just read out two or three observations. The first 
by Justice Ramaswamy is, "Suppose after general elections held, no political 
party or coalition of parties or groups is  able to secure absolute majority in 
Legislative Assembly and despite the Go vernor's exploring the alternatives, 
the situation has arisen in which no pol itical party is able to form stable 
Government, it would be a case of completely demonstrable inability of any 
political party to form a stable Government commanding the confidence of the 
majority members of the legislature.  It would be a case of failure of 
Constitutional machinery." 
116 

[11 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
What clearer Constitutional mandate or sanction do we need than 
this observation of the Supreme Court? If after a general election, no party is 
able to show the majority, it is clear demonstrable case of inability and hence 
failure of the Constitutional machinery. How this is going to be decided in the 
Raj Bhavan or in the Assembly, that is  a big question. However, their creases 
could be ironed out by conference or by  consensus of the political parties." 
So, he invited everybody. "As regards ho rse-trading by the legislators, there 
are no judicially discoverable and manageable standards to decide these 
things in judicial review. A floor-test may provide an impetus for corruption and 
rank force and violence by musclemen or  wrongful confinement or volitional 
captivity of legislators occurs till the date of the floor-t est in the House, to gain 
majority on the floor of the House." So, the Supreme Court when they state 
the virtues of the floor-test rule in Bo mmai case, they say that there would be 
exceptional situations where you keep the legislators in confinement, you use 
musclemen, you use force, in such a case, should the Governor say, "I will 
resort to floor-test."? The figures are ve ry clear; 144 say, please make so and 
so when 200 are required. The number of 200 is required and 206 say, we are 
not going to support. Not only this, ever y other judge, because it was a split 
judgement, this was Justice Ramaswam y. Justice Jeevan Reddy says, "The 
floor-test may be one consideration which the Governor may keep in view. But 
whether or not to resort to it would depend on prevailing situation. The 
possibility of horse-trading is also to be kept in view having regard to the 
prevailing political situation. It is not possible to formulate or comprehend a set 
of rules for the exercise of the power by the Governor to conduct floor-test. 
The Governor should be left free to deal with the situation according to his 
best judgement keeping in view the Co nstitution and conventions of the 
parliamentary system of  Government. Though Sarkaria Commission and 
Rajamannar Commission, headed by two distinguished Judges of this land, 
recommended floor-test, it could only mean that that is a c onsideration which 
must cross the mind of the Governor. It wo uld suffice to say that the Governor 
should be alive to the situation but he would be the sole judge of the question 
whether or not conditions are conducive to resort to floor-test." 
Even when the Justice Sarkaria recommends, the Supreme Court 
says, the Governor must know. Supposing,  in hypothetical situation, instead 
of 145, the figure was 195, probably th is observation could have persuaded 
the Governor to say that it is so much closer to the striking distance to form a 
government of 200.    Floor-test is probably the best test. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [11 MARCH, 2002]  
But if you are 25 per cent short of the half-way-mark, then t he floor test rule 
says that it is not required. These are all observations which repeatedly they

Minister losing the majority and the new Chief man is to be invited, there is a 
difference. So, the Supreme Court, even Justice Jeevan Reddy, because it is 
a majority view, says... 
"We make it clear that what we have said about is confined to a 
situation where the incumbent Chief Minister is alleged to have lost majority or

general election where the Governor has to invite the leader of the party,
